tldr: By separating balance control from task-specific motion generation and providing partial goals (prompts) through code to a single, frozen whole-body policy, this execution framework achieves diverse skills—such as walking, fall recovery, teleoperation, and sitting—without re-training policies.
hero_caption: Shows how METATRON, a single frozen base policy, generates diverse whole-body motions across both physical hardware (Unitree G1) and simulation based on input prompts (partial goals with masked targets and body parts). Flexible combinations of specified target blocks (teal) and unspecified blocks (gray) allow switching tasks without training separate policies.
overview:
When making humanoid robots perform diverse tasks, the conventional practice has been to train separate reinforcement learning policies for each task, such as locomotion, manipulation, fall recovery, and tracking control. However, basic motor skills like maintaining balance without falling and coordinating the entire body should be shared across all tasks. Training controllers from scratch for every task is inefficient, and switching between different controllers requires complex engineering.

To address this, the authors propose an architecture that cleanly separates "how to coordinate the body" from "what to achieve." A generative base policy responsible for fundamental balance and whole-body coordination is trained once and frozen. On top of it, stateful programs called "skills" govern execution. At each control step, skills pass partial goals—such as rough geometric target trajectories for the hands and feet, velocity commands, or motion styles—to the base policy as "prompts."

Evaluations on a physical Unitree G1 and a simulated character (SOMA) showed that by merely rewriting standard Python-like code without any additional policy training, the same frozen model achieved walking, getting up after falling, VR teleoperated apple pickup, sitting down and standing up from chairs, and even wall climbing and acrobatics. Furthermore, compared to conventional reference-tracking pipelines, it demonstrated significantly higher whole-body reaching success rates and push robustness.
contributions: Built a promptable generative whole-body base policy capable of flexibly accepting arbitrary partial goals, including spatio-temporal targets, relative poses, velocity commands, and style cues.
Established a large-scale distillation training pipeline integrating scene-interaction motions with object contact and synthetic recovery trajectories to handle diverse situations.

Demonstrated a framework that acquires new behaviors by generating goal prompts from ordinary code (the skill layer) written by humans or LLM coding agents, without any reinforcement learning re-training.
Demonstrated diverse task executions—such as walking, sitting, teleoperation, and autonomous recovery—from a single frozen checkpoint on both the physical Unitree G1 and in simulation.

sections.heading: Why rebuild controllers for every single task?
sections.summary: While conventional humanoid control relies on training separate reinforcement learning models for each task, it fails to share common foundations like balance and whole-body coordination. This work proposes METATRON, which freezes a single generative base policy for body coordination and elicits diverse behaviors through code-driven prompts.
sections.details:
Imagine a humanoid walking to a desk, picking up a cup at a specific time, bracing itself when pushed, handing the cup to a person, and shaking their hand. Current technology typically prepares separate pre-trained controllers for locomotion, manipulation, fall recovery, compliance control, and motion tracking, then stitches them together with handcrafted state machines. This repeatedly learns shared capabilities like balance maintenance, which is extremely inefficient.

This paper advocates for a complete separation between "what a motion should achieve (intent)" and "how to coordinate the body (physical execution)." A single general whole-body execution policy with a flexible goal specification interface is trained once, and concrete task intent is supplied every step as prompts from lightweight programs (the skill layer). Prompts can include target positions of limbs at specific times, locomotion velocity, and even motion style exemplars showing how the robot should move.

Once trained, the base policy is completely frozen. When creating a new behavior, human developers or LLM coding agents only need to write "rough geometric sketches" in code, such as target points or periodic foot trajectories. The policy interprets these sketches and automatically fills in whole-body balance and coordinated movement, turning the heavy cost of reinforcement learning re-training into a standard software engineering problem.

captions.F1: The overall concept of METATRON. A single frozen generative policy sits at the center, enabling steering, style imitation, fall recovery, teleoperation, dynamic acrobatics, and sitting on furniture across hardware and simulation, driven purely by differences in the input partial prompts.

sections.heading: The evolution from motion imitation to general-purpose controllers
sections.summary: This section traces the evolution of physics-based motion imitation and latent-space generative models to contextualize METATRON. Unlike methods requiring dense reference trajectories or task-specific re-training, METATRON excels by performing direct, real-time control from rough partial goals.
sections.details:
Recent physics-based motion imitation has evolved significantly from individual controllers tracking single motions into general trackers capable of reproducing large, diverse motion capture (Mocap) datasets. However, traditional reference tracking faces a fundamental limitation: complete reference trajectories for every joint and body link must be prepared in advance.

In contrast, latent-space generative models like ASE, CALM, and PULSE enabled downstream task adaptation by learning reusable motion representations. However, most of these methods still require training new task-specific policies for each downstream task. MaskedMimic proposed directly outputting actions from partial motion descriptions, but was limited to simple targets in simulation.

METATRON substantially extends the MaskedMimic approach. It incorporates a large-scale dataset featuring synthetic fall recoveries and furniture contacts, designs a latent space that disentangles intent from execution, reconstructs forward kinematics (FK) pose estimates purely from onboard sensors (encoders and IMU), and integrates a skill layer where LLM agents define and refine behaviors as code. Unlike methods like BeyondMimic that run heavy diffusion model optimizations at runtime, METATRON generates joint torque commands in a single feedforward pass, allowing low-latency deployment on physical humanoids.

sections.heading: How the generative base policy turns partial goals into whole-body coordination
sections.summary: Training the base policy proceeds in two stages: first, training a privileged dense motion tracker (expert) via reinforcement learning, and then distilling this expert on-policy into a student model (METATRON). Using only partial goals (prompts) and sensor history, the student generates diverse and natural whole-body motions.
sections.details:
The base policy construction pipeline incorporates several techniques to efficiently acquire robust motor skills.

### III-A Dense Motion Tracker Expert
First, an MLP policy is trained with Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) using privileged information inside the simulator (full robot state and complete future target poses $y_t$). The reward function consists of exponential penalties on joint position, orientation, and velocity tracking errors, alongside action rate regularizers that suppress sudden command changes. This phase instills high balancing ability and whole-body coordination into the expert.

### III-B Flexible Prompt Interface
The distilled student model accepts four optional goal streams along with environmental context as "prompts." Each stream includes masks, allowing unspecified body parts or items to remain completely unconstrained:
- **Spatio-temporal targets ($\mathcal{C}_t^w$)**: Positions, orientations, and arrival times for individual body parts in world coordinates. For example, commanding "place the right hand at this position after 1 second."
- **Canonical pose targets ($\mathcal{C}_t^{\ell}$)**: Local pose specifications relative to the robot's upper body and heading. Defines world-independent poses like "stand upright" or "raise hands."
- **Locomotion velocity ($u_t$)**: Directional velocity commands (m/s) without specifying target positions.
- **Style cues ($\xi_t$)**: Poses extracted from short exemplar motion clips. By deliberately collapsing temporal order into tokens, it biases behavior with motion qualities like crawling or crouching without enforcing rigid arrival times.
- **Scene information ($b_t$)**: Objects such as chairs or desks represented in local coordinates as the 8 bounding box vertices.

### III-C & D Generative Modeling via CVAE and Distillation
When given only partial goals, infinitely many whole-body movements can satisfy them (for instance, fixing only hand position leaves leg and hip angles unconstrained). Regressing a single deterministic action averages mutually incompatible solutions, leading to collapsed or unnatural poses. METATRON solves this with a conditional VAE (CVAE).

A deterministic feature extractor processes observations and prompts, while stochastic latent variables are projected onto a unit sphere ($z_t = \tilde{z}_t / \|\tilde{z}_t\|_2$) to keep the space bounded. These combine in a decoder that outputs joint targets. During distillation, data is gathered from states visited by the frozen tracker expert as well as on-policy states visited by the student responding to partial prompts. The expert's behavior is mirrored while regularizing the latent space using next-state prediction and temporal consistency losses.

sections.heading: Code generates motion: The skill layer and LLM agents manipulating prompts
sections.summary: Stateful programs that emit appropriate prompts to the frozen policy at every control step are called "skills." LLM coding agents take human-written geometric sketches, automatically refine them through simulation evaluations, and craft high-quality skill code.
sections.details:
While the base policy is capable, overly ambiguous prompts can cause unnatural behaviors, such as hesitant stepping or reluctance to shift weight when rising from a chair. The stateful programs responsible for goal-generation logic—written in Python or similar languages—form the "skill layer."

Because the base policy automatically balances and smoothly interpolates even rough targets, the skill layer does not need complex whole-body trajectory planners. Emitting elementary geometric sketches—such as straight lines, stationary setpoints, or simple periodic curves—as prompts is sufficient.

### Automated Skill Development Workflow
Skill creation relies on collaboration between humans and LLM coding agents (Figure F3):
1. A human writes coarse rules for task requirements (e.g., "sit on a chair" or "walk smoothly").
2. When the human identifies a defect (such as jittery stepping), the LLM agent constructs a test bench (playground) in simulation with varying furniture sizes, approach angles, and random target velocity sequences.
3. The agent analyzes Mocap data, fits compact geometric formulas to adjust stride and cadence, modifies and tests the code, and iteratively improves performance.

### Key Implemented Skills
- **Steering (Locomotion Control)**: Providing only velocity commands often causes short, shuffling steps. The agent derived a periodic foot-target rule that swings and lifts both feet sinusoidally based on velocity $v$ and heading angle $\alpha$. This naturally extends stride length and cadence as speed increases, enabling smooth strafing and turning.
- **Sitting and Standing**: Uses only three stationary target points derived from the chair's bounding box: a hip target slightly behind the seat center, and two foot targets in front of the seat. Without intermediate waypoints, the policy autonomously turns, approaches, and lowers its hips. Standing up works just as well with a linear target pulling the hips diagonally forward and upward.
- **Recovery**: Upon detecting a fall, the prompt switches to an upright pose or an upper-body height constraint. A simple rule that scales arrival time allowances as height recovers enables rising from any fallen configuration (Figure F4).
- **Interactive Compliance**: The robot's upper body height and heading are constrained while arm targets remain completely unspecified (masked) under zero velocity commands. Because there are no target positions to restore the arms to, the robot does not resist when a human pulls or moves its hands, enabling compliant handshakes and arm guidance.

captions.F3: The skill development workflow driven by LLM coding agents. Given task specifications and Mocap data, the agent sets up an evaluation environment and iteratively modifies skill code using simulation feedback. The base policy weights are never modified.
captions.F4: Behavior of the recovery skill. When a fall is detected, the prompt switches from steering to an upright pose target, allowing the robot to autonomously get back up. Once upright, it automatically resumes normal steering control.

sections.heading: Unifying Mocap, furniture contact, and synthetic recovery data
sections.summary: To maximize policy capabilities, the training dataset integrates large-scale Mocap data, kinematically retargeted SAMP furniture-contact motions, and synthetic recovery trajectories self-generated directly inside the simulator.
sections.details:
Training data diversity and quality are decisive factors for enabling the base policy to respond to a wide variety of prompts. This study blends three primary data sources:

### Motion Capture Retargeting
A large Mocap library (including BONES) covering daily activities, walking, dancing, sports, and acrobatics was retargeted to the humanoid's kinematic structure to provide the foundation for movement.

### Retargeting Furniture Contact Motions (SAMP)
The SAMP dataset, which features scene interactions such as sitting on chairs and lying on beds, was incorporated. Naive kinematic retargeting from humans to robots causes the robot to penetrate furniture or float unnaturally to avoid collisions.
The authors developed a two-stage optimization pipeline. The first stage optimizes joint limits and foot contacts, while the second introduces collision penalties against the furniture's surface point cloud alongside joint anchor penalties. Strictly penalizing interior penetration depth while allowing surface contact produced natural reference motions that sit properly without floating.

### Self-Generating Synthetic Recovery Motions
Human Mocap data for standing up after falling is limited and does not match the joint limits, actuator torque, or weight distribution of a robot. Therefore, the humanoid learned recovery behaviors directly in simulation. Extending prior work on Hybrid Imitation Learning (HIL), large volumes of trajectories recovering from random fallen poses were self-generated, recorded in simulation, and integrated into the training data.

sections.heading: Diverse validations and superior robustness across the G1 and simulation
sections.summary: On the physical Unitree G1, walking, teleoperation, sitting, and fall recovery were demonstrated using the exact same frozen model. Furthermore, in whole-body reaching and severe push-disturbance experiments, it substantially outperformed conventional reference-tracking pipelines in success rate and fall resistance.
sections.details:
Experiments were conducted on the physical Unitree G1 and in simulation (G1 and the high-DoF SOMA character). For hardware control, the base policy was compiled with TensorRT and CUDA graphs, sending 50 Hz joint commands over Ethernet from a GPU laptop.

### VI-B Demonstrations on Physical G1
Without modifying any policy weights, the physical Unitree G1 smoothly executed the following tasks (Figure F5):
- **Refined Steering and Locomotion**: Driven by game controller stick inputs, foot targets from the skill layer enabled forward motion, turning, and strafing with decisive, confident strides.
- **VR Headset Teleoperation**: By tracking operator hand positions with a PICO headset and directly mapping them to the robot's hand targets, the robot picked up an apple from a table.
- **Sitting on Furniture and Standing**: Given only the sofa's bounding box, the robot maneuvered around, sat down, stood back up, and walked away.
- **Autonomous Hardware Fall Recovery**: From various fallen configurations—supine, prone, or sitting on the floor—the robot stood up autonomously using only onboard sensors (Figure F7).

### VI-D Extreme Motions in Simulation
To prevent hardware damage, high-risk tests were conducted in MuJoCo simulation, demonstrating forward rolls and crawling locomotion under style cues. On the SOMA character, the same recipe completed a dynamic parkour sequence—running, sliding down a ledge, recovering from a fall, and climbing a wall—using a single frozen policy (Figure F6).

### VI-E Comparison with Reference-Tracking Pipelines
METATRON was compared against baselines combining diffusion-based whole-body reference generators (ARDY) or fast GRU generators with a SONIC tracker.
- **Whole-Body Reaching (Table I)**: In a test reaching for 54 spatial hand targets requiring stepping, crouching, or stretching, existing pipelines oscillated or collapsed trying to maintain hand positions. METATRON achieved the highest reaching success rate.
- **Pelvis Push Disturbances During Locomotion (Table II)**: External forces were applied to the pelvis from 8 directions for 100 ms while walking at 1 m/s. Baselines saw a 0% success rate (falling on all attempts) at impacts above 600 N. METATRON withstood intense 800 N and 1000 N impacts with a 75% success rate while maintaining locomotion.

### VI-F Ablation Studies
Ablations removing synthetic recovery data, latent regularization losses, or specific prompt types confirmed that the proposed auxiliary losses, synthetic data, and flexible prompt representations are critical for robustness under disturbances.

captions.F6: Dynamic behaviors of the SOMA character in simulation. Running, sliding down a cliff, recovering from a fall, and wall climbing are executed as a single continuous sequence under the same model.

sections.heading: Current limitations and future outlook
sections.summary: Key challenges include unintended behaviors triggered by out-of-distribution prompts (such as abrupt velocity spikes from rest), external dependencies on vision and planning for long-horizon autonomy, and the need for broader statistical evaluations on hardware.
sections.details:
While METATRON demonstrates remarkable flexibility, the authors highlight several limitations:

- **Motion Repertoire Coverage and Prompt Ambiguity**: Generated motions depend on the training data distribution. For example, abruptly commanding 2 m/s forward velocity from a standstill can mistakenly trigger a forward roll instead of walking. While real-world deployments smooth velocity inputs with exponential moving averages, broader data collection and skill refinement remain necessary.
- **External Dependencies for Goal Generation and Long-Horizon Planning**: Because the system focuses on being an execution layer coordinating the body for given prompts, it lacks perception pipelines or global reasoning to navigate around obstacles and identify chairs autonomously. Future work must integrate VLMs (Vision-Language Models) or high-level LLM planners for autonomous prompt generation.
- **Breadth of Hardware Evaluation**: Although diverse tasks succeeded on the physical G1, comprehensive statistical reliability evaluations covering varying floor friction, actuator thermal limits, and contact forces remain to be completed.

sections.heading: Whole-body control: Moving from re-training to programming
sections.summary: Leveraging insights from dense motion imitation, METATRON realizes a flexible, prompt-driven whole-body execution layer. Once a strong base policy is frozen, acquiring new humanoid skills becomes a software development problem of writing code, rather than re-training reinforcement learning models.
sections.details:
The core takeaway of this paper is the immense scalability gained by decoupling motor coordination ("how") from task intent ("what"). In conventional robotics, inventing a new task meant designing reward functions and running reinforcement learning in simulation for hours or days.

METATRON breaks this paradigm. It proves that once a versatile execution layer masters whole-body balance, sitting, and recovery, new tasks can be achieved instantly by writing a few lines of target formulas or letting LLMs iteratively refine code. This marks a practical, significant milestone toward treating physical intelligence as a standard software stack.

sections.heading: Appendix: Expert training setup and distributed distillation behind the scenes
sections.summary: This section describes the large-scale training setup built on Isaac Lab and ProtoMotions, detailing GPU allocations for distributed distillation across four specialist experts and network architecture hyperparameters.
sections.details:
### Distributed Distillation and Compute Resources
Training was conducted within the ProtoMotions framework built on Isaac Lab. For the G1 policy distillation, 20 GPUs ran parallel training partitioned across four expert groups: 12 GPUs for BONES, 4 for AMASS+LAFAN, 2 for recovery, and 2 for SAMP. Each GPU ran 2,048 parallel environments, synchronizing across a total batch size of 4,096 samples to update the student model's single parameter set. Control frequencies were set to 50 Hz for G1 (every 4 steps of a 200 Hz physics simulation) and 30 Hz for SOMA (every 4 steps of a 120 Hz physics simulation).

### Network Architecture
The G1 BONES tracker expert incorporates Finite Scalar Quantization (FSQ), utilizing an encoder with hidden dimensions (2048, 1024, 512, 512) and an 8-layer deep MLP actor-critic with units tapering from 4096 down to 512. In contrast, the deployable student model (METATRON) running on the robot is compressed into a compact 3-layer MLP decoder with 1024 units, enabling real-time inference on onboard hardware.

takeaways: Decoupling physical coordination (generative base policy) from task intent (skill code) allows adding new behaviors without re-training reinforcement learning policies.
Partial goals (prompts) do not require precise trajectory planning; simple geometric sketches (points or sine waves) are enough for the policy to autonomously balance and adapt stride.
LLM coding agents can write and tune skill code, turning robot motion acquisition into an iterative software development loop.
An integrated whole-body control approach exhibits far superior push recovery and reaching capabilities compared to traditional locomotion-generation plus IK-tracking pipelines.
limitations: Abrupt prompt transitions outside the training distribution (such as sudden acceleration from rest) can accidentally trigger unintended behaviors like forward rolls.
Lacks global planning and vision perception for long-distance navigation, obstacle avoidance, or autonomous chair detection, relying instead on higher-level systems.
Hardware experiments are primarily qualitative demonstrations; statistical verification of long-term failure rates across diverse surfaces and actuator limits remains future work.
